title: Showy — and whether anyone meant it
core: All four describe something that draws the eye: display, colour, decoration, standing out. They split on two axes. First, intent — is the showiness deliberate, staged for an audience, or does the thing simply stick out? Second, what gets judged — the person's motive, their flair, or the surface of the object or style itself.

words.nuance: The only one indifferent to intent: it reports visibility, not showmanship. A coffee stain, a lone red coat in a grey crowd, a missing guest — anything that fails to blend into its surroundings qualifies, and a *conspicuous* thing may be desperately trying not to be noticed.

Convicts the motive, not the thing. It says the display exists to be admired — which is why it works on virtue as easily as money: **ostentatious** piety, grief, modesty. Call something this and you have accused someone of performing.

The one you can be complimented with. It reads as flair owned and enjoyed — a conductor, a waistcoat, a signature — and it imputes no insincerity and no vulgarity, only theatre. The showiness entertains rather than solicits.

Attaches to surfaces and styles, not to people's behaviour: prose, music, ornament clotted with flourishes until the sense drowns. Uniquely in this group it also has a purely physical sense — a red, flushed complexion — with no display involved at all.

exam_note: The trap is treating them as interchangeable "showy" synonyms: **conspicuous** needs no performer, **florid** needs no person, and only **flamboyant** can be praise.
